nameStory: The concentric pelt lichen gets its name from the distinctive circular, ring-like patterns that form on its surface as it grows outward from the center. Like other pelt lichens, it resembles a flattened animal hide or pelt spread across the ground. The species name 'elisabethae' honors a botanist named Elisabeth, though the exact person commemorated is lost to scientific history.
description: Concentric pelt lichen is a medium-sized, leafy lichen that grows flat against soil and moss like a leathery mat. It typically reaches 4-8 inches across and displays beautiful concentric rings or zones of different colors radiating outward from the center. The upper surface is usually grayish-green when dry, turning brighter green when wet. This uncommon lichen is one of New England's rarest pelt lichens, making any sighting special.

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Look for distinctive concentric rings or zones of color that create a bull's-eye pattern across the surface, often with alternating bands of lighter and darker tones

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms broad, flat, leafy lobes that feel leathery and flexible when moist, like soft suede or chamois cloth

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Gray-green to brownish-gray when dry, becoming vibrant green when wet, with the concentric zones becoming more pronounced with moisture

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Always grows on soil, moss, or decaying organic matter, never on rock or tree bark

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Medium-sized specimens typically 4-8 inches across, though older individuals can reach up to a foot in diameter

habitat: Found in shaded, moist areas of mature forests, particularly on rich humus soil among mosses and forest floor debris. Prefers cool, humid environments with consistent moisture, often in north-facing slopes or ravines. In New England, it's most likely encountered in old-growth or mature second-growth deciduous and mixed forests.

seasonality.spring: Most vibrant during wet spring weather when the concentric patterns show maximum contrast and the surface becomes bright green. This is often the best time for photography and detailed observation.
seasonality.summer: May appear duller and more brownish during dry periods, but maintains its diagnostic ring pattern. Look for it in consistently moist microhabitats during summer droughts.
seasonality.fall: Often refreshed by autumn rains, returning to more vibrant coloration. The concentric zones may be particularly visible against fallen leaves.
seasonality.winter: Remains visible under light snow cover, appearing gray-brown but still showing the telltale ring pattern. Snow melt provides good viewing opportunities.

funFact: This lichen is so rare in New England that each specimen you find might be decades or even centuries old - lichen growth is incredibly slow, with some large specimens adding less than a millimeter of growth per year, making them among the oldest living organisms you can easily observe in the forest.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other pelt lichens, but the concentric ring pattern is diagnostic - no other New England pelt lichen shows this bull's-eye arrangement. Remember: 'concentric circles = concentric pelt' to distinguish it from the more common dog pelt lichen, which has a more uniform surface.
contextualKnowledge: The extreme rarity of this species in New England (only 6 recorded observations) means that any sighting should be photographed and potentially reported to local naturalist groups or iNaturalist. Its scarcity may be due to habitat loss, air pollution sensitivity, or climate change impacts on the specific conditions it requires.
compareHints: Unlike the common dog pelt lichen which has a relatively uniform surface with veins on the underside, concentric pelt lichen displays obvious ring patterns on top. It differs from freckled pelt lichen by lacking the small, dark, pimple-like structures (cephalodia) scattered across the surface. The horizontal pelt lichen grows in overlapping shelves rather than flat rings, making the growth pattern a reliable distinguishing feature.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the pelt lichens, scaly pelt is the only one in New England with prominent phyllidia scattered across its surface.

Among the many pelt lichens in New England, horizontal pelt lichen is unique for its completely prostrate growth habit - it never curls up at the edges like dog pelt lichen or forms the ruffled, frilly margins of freckled pelt lichen.
Distinguished from dog pelt lichen by having many more fruiting structures along the edges rather than just a few large ones.

Among the many pelt lichens in New England, dog pelt lichen stands out for its preference for growing directly on soil rather than trees, and its particularly well-defined dark veining on a pale underside.
Among the pelt lichens, ruffled freckled pelt stands out for its notably bumpy, textured surface and strongly ruffled edges.
Unlike all other pelt lichens in New England, Eastern Waterfan is the only one that lives in water rather than on soil, rocks, or trees in terrestrial habitats.
Unlike the more common dog pelt lichen which has evenly-spaced, rounded lobes, alternating dog lichen has its distinctive alternating finger-like projections along the edges.
Among the pelt lichens, freckled pelt is the only one with distinctive dark green cephalodia (freckles), making identification fairly straightforward.
Unlike the common dog pelt lichen which has a smooth surface, peppered pelt is distinguished by its dark spotted pattern.
Among its pelt lichen relatives, sheepish pelt lichen is distinguished by its uniquely woolly surface texture - most other Peltigera species have smooth or slightly wrinkled surfaces.
